A human-made public messenger and announcer — an official role for broadcasting messages, proclamations, and formal communications to an audience. Built to persist through institutional appointment, ritualized speech acts, and the social practice of public proclamation.

A notary is a human-made officer of public record, appointed or licensed to witness acts, authenticate documents, and certify facts — an institution built to extend trust across time and distance by embedding individual credibility into a recognized office.

A human-made convention: a prescribed sequence of ritual actions, words, and gestures. The word 'liturgy' does not name any natural phenomenon — it names a cultural technology for structuring repeated ceremonial practice. Built to persist through textual transmission, teaching, and institutional reinforcement.

A steward is a human-made role and institution: a person or entity entrusted with the management of property, affairs, or resources on behalf of another. The concept exists only within social, legal, and economic systems — it is a construct of trust, obligation, and delegated authority, not a natural phenomenon.
A human-made institutional role: an officer of the court or legislature entrusted with maintaining order, serving processes, and enforcing directives on behalf of the authorizing body.

A palimpsest is a human-made manuscript page or tablet that has been scraped clean of its original text so it can be reused, a physical practice of writing-surviving-through-erasure. The natural material (parchment, clay, wax) is not the construct — the practice of systematic scraping and rewriting is.

A proviso is a human-made conditional clause appended to a statement, agreement, law, or resolution. It restricts, qualifies, or adds conditions to what it accompanies. Built to persist through legal drafting conventions and language — it is a structural element of human communication in formal contexts.

Human-made annotations, notes, and comments written in the margins of books and manuscripts. Created by readers, scholars, and scribes as a practice of engagement with texts — a physical record of interpretation, correction, and dialogue across time.

A colophon is a brief statement at the end of a book or manuscript giving details of its production, publication, or authorship. It is a human-made paratextual device used for centuries to document provenance, printer identity, and production circumstances of a book.

A human-made concept for formal warning or caution — the practice of alerting others (especially authorities) to potential issues and requesting that action be suspended until the cautioner can present their case. Built to persist through legal registers, official notices, and institutional memory across generations of legal practice.

A human-made textual artifact: a short quotation, saying, or phrase placed at the beginning of a book, chapter, or other work to set tone, provide context, or pay homage. Also used as an inscription on buildings, statues, or coins. Created by authors, publishers, and artisans; persists through publication and physical inscription.
A handwritten or typewritten document, before it is printed or published. Created by human authors and scribes, persisted through copying, archiving, and institutional custody.

Incipit is a human-made convention of manuscript production: the opening words or phrase of a written work, marked out from the body text by decoration, special script, or spatial separation. It is an artifact of human editorial practice — scribes and booksellers produce incipits to help readers identify, locate, and begin a text. Built to persist through scribal reproduction and cataloguing.

errata is a human-made list of errors discovered in a published work alongside their corrections. It is created by authors, editors, or publishers to maintain the accuracy of a text after initial publication, and persists through errata sheets, online correction pages, and updated editions.

A gloss is a human-made annotation — a brief explanatory note added alongside a text to clarify, interpret, or expand upon difficult or obscure passages. Scribes and scholars have produced glosses since antiquity, inscribing them in margins, interlines, or compiled into separate marginalia volumes. It is built to persist through copying, teaching, and the transmission of texts across generations.

A human-made judicial mechanism — a writ ordering that a detained person be brought before a court to examine the legality of the detention. Created by English common law, codified in statutes worldwide, enforced by judicial order. It is a construct of legal procedure, not a natural phenomenon.

A human-made convention in manuscript and early book production: a word or short phrase printed at the foot of a page, serving as a guide for correct page sequencing and as a verification aid during collation. Built to persist through scribal practice, printing conventions, and library cataloging systems.

A human-made scholarly abbreviation or symbol used to identify manuscripts, authors, editions, or other sources in bibliographic and textual-critical work. Created and maintained by the academic community to compress references and enable precise citation across languages and scripts.

A recension is a human-made practice of critical examination and revision of texts, especially in scholarly editing. It emerges from the systematic work of textual critics who compare manuscript variants to produce an edited text. The practice is built to persist through the conventions of academic publishing, critical apparatuses, and the ongoing revision of scholarly editions across generations of textual scholarship.

A model manuscript produced as a reference copy for scribes to replicate. Human-made through the scribal practice of producing archetype texts — carefully produced, corrected master copies from which other copies are made. Built to persist through the institutional practice of archival preservation in monasteries, scriptoria, and libraries.

A codicil is a human-made legal instrument — a written supplement to a last will and testament that modifies provisions without revoking the entire will. It is created by human legal practice to enable testamentary changes without drafting an entirely new will, persisting through notarial execution and court filing in probate.
a formal systematic written discourse on a subject, produced by human scholarship and built to persist through written record, institutional reproduction, and citation networks

explanatory or analytical writing that works through another text — interpreting, annotating, or debating its meaning — built to persist through scholarly tradition, manuscript reproduction, and citation networks

A scholium is a scholarly commentary or explanatory note added to a text, typically in the margin or between lines of a manuscript. It is a human-made annotation practice originating in classical antiquity and persisting through medieval and early modern textual transmission, built to persist as a convention of scholarly engagement with source texts.

a conventional notation marking the end of a written text in manuscript culture, created by scribes and authors to signal completion — a human-made textual marker built to persist through scribal practice and book production

A motion is a formal request made to a court or judge for a specific ruling or order. It is a human-made procedural instrument: written or oral submissions that trigger judicial action. Without courts and procedural rules, there is no motion — only requests.

A legend is a human-made explanatory key that maps symbols, colors, or markings in a diagram or map to their meanings. Built to persist as a convention enabling any viewer to decode visual information

A lemma is a short excerpt of text quoted for the purpose of commentary — a human-made editorial practice dating to ancient scholarship. Scribes and scholars deliberately extract and reproduce passages as anchors for exegesis, glosses, and scholia. Built to persist through manuscript transmission and scholarly convention.

A human-made category for deviations from expected patterns — the concept of anomaly is a classificatory tool built by science, statistics, and quality practice to flag observations that resist prediction within a given model.

A human-made institutional guarantee: the requirement that the state respect all legal rights owed to a person, following established procedures before depriving them of life, liberty, or property. It is the map of procedural fairness in legal systems.

The concept of a point of no return — a threshold action or decision beyond which one cannot retreat without loss. Originally from the historical crossing of the Rubicon river by Julius Caesar, now a general human-made metaphorical concept embedded in language, rhetoric, and culture. The entry names the MAP, not the river.

The formal process of resolving disputes through a judicial or quasi-judicial procedure — a human-made institution of law, not a natural capacity. Built to persist through codified rules, trained practitioners, and institutional memory.

A human-made scholarly apparatus: the critical notes, variants, and explanatory material attached to a text to guide its reading and interpretation. Built to persist through editorial practice and textual criticism.

Acquittal is a formal legal declaration by a court that a defendant is not guilty of the charges against them. It is a human-made judicial act that terminates criminal proceedings in favor of the accused, built to persist through legal records and precedent.

The human practice of assembling and arranging texts, manuscripts, or documents in their correct order by comparing multiple copies or fragments. A made-side editorial discipline that persists through the explicit practices of scribes, editors, and archivists who sequence leaves, folios, or pages into a coherent whole.
A synopsis is a human-made brief summary or survey of a larger work, created by authors, editors, and publishers to compress and convey the contents of a text, film, or other media to an audience.

Tagging is the human practice of attaching labels to artifacts for later retrieval and organization. It is a cognitive and social technology for creating ad hoc classification systems, used across physical and digital domains.

A foundational proposition accepted as true within a formal system, serving as a starting point for reasoning and derivation. Human-made as a methodological choice — the selection of axioms is a deliberate act of convention that structures entire deductive frameworks and persists through teaching, formalization, and the systems they ground.

The material, channel, or system through which content is transmitted, expressed, or rendered — a human invention for carrying meaning across distance, time, or modality. Every medium is a design choice that shapes what can be communicated and how it is received.

A formal legal document that charges a person with a serious crime, issued by a prosecutorial authority on behalf of the state. It is the human-made mechanism that initiates formal criminal prosecution, distinguishing accusatory process from mere suspicion.

human-made textual practice — a copy or transcript of a document, especially one made from memory or without consulting the original source. Built to persist through scholarly convention and cataloging systems.

A human-made legal institution: the rule in adjudicative proceedings that assigns which party must produce evidence to support their claims. The map of allocatio probationis — a procedural construct built by law to decide cases when facts are disputed. Purely human, institutional, and persisting through codified procedure and judicial practice.

corollary is a human-made epistemic concept in mathematics and formal discourse — a proposition that follows directly from a proved theorem, requiring little additional argument. It is a device for packaging deductive consequences as standalone claims.

Pragmatics is a human-made discipline within linguistics: the study of how context — speaker intent, shared knowledge, situational factors — shapes meaning beyond literal semantic content. It is a conceptual framework built by linguists and philosophers to explain how communication works in practice.

Discovery is the human-made legal procedure by which parties in a dispute exchange relevant information and evidence before trial. It is a structured institutional mechanism — not natural communication, but a rule-governed process for compelling disclosure.

Presumption is a human-made epistemic and legal mechanism — a rule that treats an unproven fact as established unless rebutted. It is a convention of reasoning and evidence, not a statement about how the world actually is. Humans invented presumptions to manage uncertainty in legal, institutional, and everyday reasoning, and they persist through codification, teaching, and practice.

A human-made concept for a systematic tendency to favor, interpret, or weight information in a particular direction. Not the natural tendency itself but the map — the category humans built to identify, diagnose, and correct predictable deviations in judgment, perception, and memory.

A human-made method of reasoning by mapping structural relationships from a known domain (source) onto an unfamiliar domain (target). Built to persist through teaching, textual transmission, rhetorical practice, and computational implementation.

argumentation is the structured human practice of constructing and exchanging reasons to support claims. It is a human-made cognitive and social technology — built to persist through language, teaching, and institutional rules — that enables collective reasoning, persuasion, and dispute resolution. The natural side offers raw inference; argumentation is the made artifact that organizes inference into accountable exchange.

The standard-of-proof is a human-invented threshold that specifies how much evidence is required to establish a proposition as true in a given domain. It is a norm governing inference, not a natural fact — it varies across domains (law, science, daily life) and exists only because humans create procedures for deciding what counts as settled.

A human-made mechanism for constraining one's future choices to align with present goals. It is a deliberate intervention across time — a self-binding strategy that sacrifices future flexibility to secure present intent. Found in law (contracts, trusts, irrevocable mandates), economics (savings commitments, penalty contracts), psychology (implementation intentions, commitment devices), and ritual (vows, oaths, pledges). The natural self does not precommit; only the human capacity for temporal self-modeling and rule-making enables it.

A human-made concept from social psychology describing the mental discomfort experienced when holding contradictory beliefs, values, or commitments — a map of a cognitive tension, not the tension itself

The human-made capacity to assess whether a source, claim, or entity is worthy of belief — a taxonomy of trustworthiness built through language, discipline, and social practice, not a natural faculty.

The epistemic practice of questioning claims and requiring evidence before acceptance. A human-made framework for evaluating the strength of belief against available justification — not doubt itself, but the methodical procedure of suspended judgment.

A human-made psychological concept: the process of constructing plausible explanations for decisions, behaviors, or beliefs after the fact. Created by psychologists and sociologists to describe how humans maintain self-consistency through narrative — it exists in discourse, teaching, and clinical practice, not as a natural faculty.

Calibration is the human-made practice of aligning an instrument, measure, or judgment against a known standard. It is a procedure created by metrology and epistemology to reduce systematic error, and persists through institutional protocols, traceable standards, and the disciplined habit of periodic re-verification.

A simplified and overgeneralized representation of a category of people, objects, or events — projecting assumed attributes without regard for individual variation. Human-made as a cognitive category, persisting through language, social teaching, and cultural transmission.

A human-made cognitive pattern — the documented tendency for people to selectively gather, interpret, and recall information in ways that confirm their preexisting beliefs. It is a construct of cognitive psychology, named and operationalized in research by Nickerson (1998) and others, persisting through academic literature, teaching, and public discourse.
the systematic act of counting or listing items individually to track, quantify, and organize discrete entities; a human cognitive practice formalized through notation, registries, and databases.

The human-made cognitive bias whereby initial information (the anchor) disproportionately influences subsequent judgments and decisions. The map is the category humans built to pick out this systematic error in quantitative estimation and decision-making.

A human-made practice of reducing complexity in information, processes, or representations to make them accessible, usable, or communicable. Built to persist through techniques, protocols, and cultural transmission.

A human-made concept in cognitive psychology naming the systematic tendency to judge the likelihood or importance of events by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by actual statistical frequency

A human-made concept in political science and sociology describing how dominant groups maintain control not through force but through manufactured consent — shaping culture, norms, and institutions so their rule appears natural. It is the map of a power dynamic, not the power itself; the concept persists through academic discourse, critical pedagogy, and institutional critique.

Human-made mapping between meaning and form — a scheme for representing information through systematic transformation into symbols, signals, or structures. Built to persist through shared conventions, standards bodies, and taught protocols.

A cognitive bias in human judgment: the tendency for people to react differently to the same information depending on how it is presented (framed). Human-made because it is a concept in psychology and behavioral economics that categorizes a systematic pattern of decision-making distortion, persisted through academic literature, teaching, and clinical practice.

A human-made pedagogical and analytic construct for organizing concepts at successive levels of generality and specificity. It is the map of abstraction levels, not abstraction itself — a framework humans built to make explicit the distance between concrete instances and abstract categories, enabling deliberate navigation between detail and generality in communication, design, and reasoning.

A human-made cognitive bias: the tendency to continue investing in a failing course of action because of previously invested resources (time, money, effort). It is a pattern of reasoning that humans have identified, named, and catalogued in psychology — the map of a systematic error in human judgment, not the natural impulse itself.

A nudge is a human-made behavioral intervention that alters decisions or actions without forbidding options or significantly changing incentives. It is a designed feature of choice architecture, not a natural phenomenon — the concept was formalized by Thaler and Sunstein as a tool for steering behavior within libertarian paternalism.

A belief-bias is a human-made concept from cognitive psychology naming the tendency to judge the strength of arguments by the plausibility of their conclusions rather than by logical validity. It is a documented, measured phenomenon in experimental psychology — a construct of the scientific map, not the raw behavior itself.

The practice of monitoring, evaluating, and regulating one's own cognitive processes. Human-made as a psychological construct — it does not name the faculty of thought itself but the structured awareness of thinking as an object of thought, formalized in cognitive science and educational practice.

Social friction is a human-made concept describing the resistance, effort, and drag that accumulate in social interactions, institutional processes, and collective coordination. It is not a natural force but a constructed category — a way of describing why things that should be easy become hard, and why systems require energy to keep moving. The concept persists through language, management practice, and policy design.

anchoring-bias is a human-made psychological construct describing a systematic pattern in human judgment and decision-making -- the tendency to rely too heavily on initial information (the anchor) when making subsequent judgments. It is a concept developed in cognitive psychology to categorize and predict a reproducible error in estimation. As a taxonomic map of human reasoning, it persists through empirical research, pedagogical transmission in psychology and behavioral economics, and its operationalization in decision science and public policy interventions.

a human-made agricultural implement consisting of a long handle with a short blade set at right angles, designed for breaking up soil, removing weeds, and cultivating earth — an object produced by tool-making traditions spanning millennia across independent cultures worldwide

The optimism bias is a human-made psychological concept — a map that categorizes the tendency for people to systematically overestimate the likelihood of positive outcomes and underestimate negative ones. It is a construct of cognitive psychology, not the feelings themselves.

A figure of speech and cognitive mechanism where one concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it — e.g. 'the White House' for the US executive branch, or 'crown' for monarchy. Human-made as a linguistic convention and a conceptual shortcut, persisted through teaching in rhetoric, literature, and everyday communication.

A cognitive shortcut where people estimate the frequency or probability of events by how easily examples come to mind. A human-made psychological construct developed by Tversky and Kahneman in 1973 to categorize a systematic bias in human judgment under uncertainty. The concept itself is made — the category, the operationalization, the experimental paradigms — all output of the behavioral science research program.
Human-made cognitive taxonomy: the map distinguishing the systematic tendency for negative stimuli to weigh more heavily than equivalent positive ones in judgment and memory.

The mental model of spatial or topological relationships that humans build to navigate physical environments and abstract structures. It is a constructed representational capacity, not innate geography — shaped by culture, language, and deliberate cartographic practice. Humans make maps of cities, of social networks, of conceptual taxonomies; the map is the construct, not the territory it represents.

The human-made tendency to weight recent information more heavily than older data when making judgments or decisions. This is a feature of the cognitive architecture humans operate within — not a moral failing but a systematic distortion of memory retrieval and attention, documented in experimental psychology and organizational behavior studies.

A human-constructed framework in cognitive psychology that quantifies the total mental effort required to perform a task, measured by working-memory demands, attentional resources, and processing capacity. Built to persist through empirical methodology, peer review, and integration into educational and interface design.

A human-made psychological construct describing a limited-capacity system for temporarily holding and manipulating information. Built to persist through cognitive theory, experimental paradigms (span tasks, dual-task interference), and computational models of cognition. The map, not the faculty itself.

A human-made cognitive framework that structures thought about one domain in terms of another (e.g. argument-as-war). Created by Lakoff and Johnson as a theory of embodied cognition — it is a map of how metaphor operates in reasoning, not the natural act of imagining.

Priming is a human-made cognitive-psychological construct: the concept that exposure to one stimulus systematically influences the response to a subsequent stimulus. It is a theoretical framework developed in experimental psychology to categorize and predict how prior mental activation shapes behavior. The natural phenomenon is the brain's associative readiness; priming is the map.

A formal mode of inference introduced by Charles Sanders Peirce, describing how agents generate explanatory hypotheses from incomplete observations. Human-made: a logical concept formalized in philosophy and science, not a natural cognitive tendency.

Hindsight bias (the 'knew-it-all-along' effect) is a human-made cognitive category: a named pattern of retrospective distortion where people misremember their prior predictions as having been obvious. It persists through experimental protocols, clinical practice, and legal testimony review — a map built to catch the gap between memory and certainty.

The human-constructed norm of aligning one's beliefs with available evidence — distinguished from instrumental rationality (goal achievement). A standard for truth-conducive belief formation, maintained through scientific practice, evidential norms, and epistemic education. Law 2a: this is the map of the standard, not the natural cognitive faculties themselves.

Belief-persistence is the human-made psychological concept describing how beliefs endure despite counterevidence or disconfirmation. It is a construct from cognitive psychology and social science, built through research paradigms, theoretical models, and academic discourse to classify a pattern of human reasoning behavior.

A human-made concept in epistemology and systems theory: a feedback mechanism wherein the output of a knowledge-forming process feeds back as input to that process, enabling self-correction, self-reinforcement, or self-undermining. Built to persist through formal logic, scientific methodology, and reflective reasoning practices.

A human-made category of systematic errors that occur in deliberate reasoning processes — distinct from perceptual or memory biases. Built to persist through education, critical thinking instruction, and the formal study of logic and decision-making.

A meta-category is a human-made classification layer that groups other categories together. Humans create taxonomies to organize knowledge, and meta-categories are the higher-order categories that organize those taxonomies themselves — the categories of categories. This is a made construct: no natural kind exists 'above' kinds; it is purely a human intellectual technology for structuring how we structure what we know.

chunking is the human-made cognitive mechanism of grouping individual information units into larger, meaningful clusters — a concept from cognitive psychology that maps how expertise compresses working memory load through pattern recognition and structured recall.

Denotation is a human-made semiotic concept: the direct, literal relationship between a sign and what it refers to. It is a construct of meaning theory, developed in linguistics, semiotics, and philosophy of language to distinguish literal reference from associative or contextual meaning.

The human-made concept of a mechanism that shapes behavior through anticipated consequences. Not the natural reflex itself, but the socially constructed framework — rewards, penalties, signals — that humans design to align individual action with collective or institutional outcomes.

Connotation is a human-made semantic concept — the secondary associations, emotional overtones, and contextual meanings that a word, symbol, or sign carries beyond its literal denotation. It is the interpretive layer that humans build around signs through culture, experience, and shared practice. The concept persists through language teaching, literary criticism, and semiotic analysis.

Reinforcement is a human-made concept from behavioral science — a process by which consequences following a behavior alter the future probability of that behavior occurring. It is not a natural force but a theoretical construct built through observation, experimentation, and systematic modification of organism-environment relationships. The concept persists through teaching, research protocols, and applied practice in fields ranging from education to clinical therapy.

Human-made strategy of delegating cognitive work to external artifacts — notes, diagrams, calculators, calendars — to augment finite biological memory and attention. Built to persist through cultural transmission of tool-use practices and formal instruction in cognitive strategies.

Jargon is the specialized vocabulary and usage patterns of a particular group, trade, or discipline. It is human-made because it is produced through collective linguistic practice — not natural language but a filtered, technical, or insider register built by humans to signal membership, achieve precision, or exclude outsiders within a social group.

A human-made learning technique that schedules review of material at increasing intervals to exploit the psychological spacing effect, persisting through educational practice, instructional systems, and algorithmic flashcard systems.
a human-made linguistic construct: a fixed phrase whose meaning cannot be derived from the literal meanings of its constituent words, preserved through cultural transmission and teaching

A human-made cognitive strategy in learning and memory — the practice of connecting new information to existing knowledge through elaborative encoding. Not the natural act of thinking deeply, but a taught technique for deeper processing.

A colloquialism is a human-made linguistic construct — an informal word or expression characteristic of everyday spoken language rather than formal or technical speech. It exists as a convention of register, persisting through teaching and social practice within speech communities.
A written document used for formal internal communication within organizations, governments, and institutions — a human-made instrument of organizational memory and coordination.

A human-made cognitive learning technique: organizing study or practice by mixing different topics or types of problems within a single session, rather than blocking on one topic. Created by cognitive scientists to improve long-term retention and transfer — it is the map of a study design, not the natural process of learning itself.

A neologism is a human-made linguistic construct: a newly coined word, phrase, or usage introduced into a language by human convention and social adoption. It exists as a map of linguistic innovation, not the natural act of speaking.

Exegesis is the human-made practice of systematically interpreting a text — especially legal, religious, or canonical documents — according to established rules and traditions. It does not exist in nature; it is an institutional technique built through centuries of interpretive communities, scholarly methods, and cultural transmission. The map of how to read and explain texts is entirely a human construct.

A human-made learning technique where learners actively recall information from memory rather than passively re-reading it. Created by educational researchers to improve long-term retention through deliberate recall exercises.

A human-made information artifact produced about an action or outcome to inform future behavior. Created by teachers, systems, peers, and instruments to reduce uncertainty and guide improvement across learning, work, and skill acquisition.

A human-made explanatory note attached to a text, image, or artifact to clarify, interpret, or critique it. Created by readers, scholars, and editors to make meaning explicit; persists through marginalia, digital comments, and scholarly apparatus.

A default is a human-made preset — a designated outcome that applies when no active choice is made. It exists only because rules, interfaces, or institutions were constructed to designate it, and it persists through those same constructions: software code, legal forms, policy manuals, and social conventions that all require human maintenance to remain in effect.

A human-made pedagogical practice in which ongoing evaluation is embedded within instruction to provide feedback and adjust teaching — not to rank or sort students but to guide learning in real time. Built to persist through rubrics, teacher training, and institutional assessment cycles.

A lexeme is the abstract minimal unit of lexical meaning in a language — a vocabulary item that can undergo inflection. It is a theoretical construct of linguistics, human-made to describe and analyze the building blocks of vocabulary across languages.

A concluding section of a literary work, authored by the writer to close the narrative or argument. It is human-made — a structural device of composition, not a natural phenomenon — designed to persist as part of the work's architecture across editions and readings.

A human-made learning technique that generates explanatory explanations by asking why questions, connecting new information to prior knowledge. Built to persist through instructional design and educational practice.

A cognitive framework constructed by humans (Fauconnier & Turner) to explain how people combine elements from different mental spaces into new integrated meanings — a map of meaning-making, not the meanings themselves.

A human-made practice of condensing a longer work into a shorter form while preserving its essential content. Built to persist through editorial craft, publishing standards, and the transmission of summarized knowledge across audiences who lack time for the full text.

dual-coding is a human-made cognitive theory by Allan Paivio (1971) proposing that information is processed through two distinct channels — verbal and visual-spatial. The theory itself, its parameters, and its educational applications are human constructs.

A human-made linguistic construct: a memorable, often distinctive phrase coined or popularized by a person, brand, or work, designed to be reproduced and recognized. Persistent through cultural transmission, media, and repeated use — it lives in language and collective memory.

human-made apparatus that frames and presents a text to readers — titles, covers, marginalia, footnotes, forewords, blurbs, and editorial conventions. Built to persist through publishing practice and literary discourse.

A pedagogical technique in which learners study step-by-step solutions to problems before attempting similar problems independently. Human-made as a structured instructional method designed to reduce cognitive load during skill acquisition.

A human-made linguistic concept: the distinctive language patterns — vocabulary, pronunciation, grammar, idiom — unique to a single individual speaker. Coined in linguistics to describe how each person's speech variety differs from group-level registers and dialects.

A human-made pedagogical method in which a learner engages in structured, goal-directed activity specifically designed to improve performance in areas of weakness, with immediate feedback and repetition at the edge of ability.

A human-made document artifact — a supplemental text appended to an existing written work after its main composition, preserving the original while adding new material. Built to persist through formal attachment to the parent document.

a human-made linguistic technique: restating a source text in one's own words while preserving meaning. It persists through language practice, education in writing, and translation — a skill taught and refined across cultures, not a natural faculty.

Human-made: the practice of alternating between two or more language varieties within a single conversation or interaction. Built to persist through sociolinguistic teaching, ethnographic documentation, and the everyday social navigation it enables.

Peritext is a human-made institutional concept from narratology (Gérard Genette) that designates the paratextual materials located within the physical boundaries of a published work — title page, table of contents, chapter headings, page numbering, running headers — which together form an institutional threshold guiding the reader from the paratextual exterior into the text proper. It is a map of how publishing culture organizes access to written content.

A human-made cognitive technique — the practice of actively expanding and enriching encoded information by connecting new material to existing knowledge, asking why, and generating examples. Built to persist through teaching, study guides, and pedagogical training.

A human-made sociolinguistic concept describing a stable speech community where two distinct language varieties coexist with strictly divided social functions — a high (H) variety for formal contexts and a low (L) variety for everyday communication. Coined by Charles Ferguson in 1959 as an analytical framework, it persists through linguistic description, teaching, and sociolinguistic research.

The explicat is a human-made convention: the concluding words, formula, or marker placed at the end of a manuscript or text to signal its termination. It is a deliberate textual artifact, part of the paratextual apparatus that frames written works from their opening (incipit) to their close.
A self-regulated learning strategy in which learners generate explanations of the material they are studying, connecting new information to prior knowledge and monitoring their own understanding

a human-made concept for a word, pronunciation, or custom that tests group membership and draws boundaries between insiders and outsiders; created as a category of social-linguistic identification, persisted through oral tradition, written records, and the social enforcement of linguistic norms

A human-made cognitive learning strategy in which learners actively connect new information to their existing knowledge structures, building richer mental models through deliberate cross-referencing of ideas across domains

Human-made practice in publishing and printing: the deliberate visual arrangement of text, images, and whitespace on a page. It is an output of editorial and design work, not a natural phenomenon — it exists only through human craft in typesetting, page layout, and graphic design.
A rhetorical figure in which a part stands for the whole (or vice versa), human-made as a linguistic device of representation, persisting through speech, writing, and literature.

a figure of speech in which the word phonetically imitates the sound it describes — a human-made linguistic device built to persist through language teaching, literature, and onomatopoeic coinage across cultures

A psychological construct invented by Lev Vygotsky to describe the space between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance. It is a human-made map used in educational theory — not the natural learning process itself, but the conceptual framework that teachers use to locate where instruction will be most effective. Built to persist through pedagogical practice, curriculum design, and teacher training.
A laptop computer designed, manufactured, and marketed by Apple Inc. as part of the MacBook product line. Human-made hardware product built to persist as a commercial technology product.

The practice of constructing or creating from whatever materials are at hand. A human-made creative strategy that persists through cultural transmission, apprenticeship, and the accumulated knowledge of what can be assembled from scrap, salvage, and repurposed parts.

A pedagogical technique in which the scaffolding support provided to a learner is systematically reduced over time, transferring responsibility for the task from instructor to learner. It is human-made, emerging from educational psychology and instructional design, and persists through teaching curricula and teacher training.

A cognitive error in which an abstract concept, relational pattern, or nominal category is treated as if it were a concrete, independently existing entity. Present across philosophy, law, sociology, and everyday reasoning.

A worked-example is a human-made pedagogical construct: a step-by-step solved problem presented by an instructor or textbook to demonstrate the procedure for solving a class of problems. It is designed to reduce cognitive load on learners by externalizing expert problem-solving steps, allowing novices to encode solution schemas without the burden of search. Built to persist through textbooks, instructional software, and teaching practice.

A human-made rhetorical device — a figure of speech in which a single word is applied to two or more others in different senses. It is a linguistic construct created by human rhetoric and preserved through literary tradition, teaching, and language.

A human-made learning strategy where practice continues beyond initial mastery to strengthen retention and build resistance to forgetting. Built to persist through structured repetition and spaced review protocols.

A diacritic is a human-made mark or symbol added to a written letter to modify its pronunciation, distinguish homographs, or indicate grammatical distinctions. It is a feature of orthographic systems — a deliberate, conventional addition to the written form of language, persisted through typography, pedagogy, and digital encoding standards.

A human-made rhetorical and linguistic concept: the use of a word in a way that departs from its conventional meaning, often through strained metaphor or deliberate 'misuse' to fill a semantic gap. Built to persist through language, rhetorical teaching, and literary tradition — it is the map of how humans navigate meaning when language runs out.

A human-designed learning strategy in which different topics or types of problems are mixed during study sessions rather than blocked by category. Built to persist through educational practice and cognitive science research.

A human-made linguistic operation: the insertion of a morpheme or word into another word, splitting it into parts. Created by speakers to add expressive force, and persists through replication in speech, writing, and literary convention.

A cognitive science concept identifying learning conditions that create initial processing difficulty but produce stronger, more durable long-term retention — a human-made framework for optimizing training design by leveraging the paradox that effortful retrieval enhances memory consolidation.

A manuscript practice in which a scribe appends a note at the end of a codex or scroll, recording the scribe's name, the place of copying, the date, and often a prayer or curse. It is a human-made convention of book production that persists through scribal tradition, library cataloguing, and scholarly editing.

Human-made: the concept of data collected, stored, and processed by organizations but never used for any operational or analytical purpose. It persists through data governance practices, compliance regimes, and the economics of digital storage.

A pedagogical strategy for note-taking and learning where learners actively reorganize and restructure incoming information rather than passively copying it. Human-made as a deliberate instructional method designed to produce deeper understanding through generative processing.
A rule of evidence that excludes out-of-court statements offered for their truth — human-made to ensure reliability through oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation.

the human-made concept describing how learned knowledge or skills apply across different contexts — a construct of educational and cognitive psychology used to study, design for, and improve learning outcomes

A formal concluding section of a speech or discourse, structured by rhetorical convention to evoke emotional response and summarize argument. A human-made rhetorical construct, not the emotion itself but the map of how closure is engineered.

A human-made rhetorical and philosophical device — the formal expression of paradox or perplexity to stimulate inquiry. The word comes from Greek ἀπορία (no passage, difficulty) and denotes a construct of human thought, not natural confusion.

Hendiadys is a human-made rhetorical device — a deliberate linguistic construction in which two words connected by conjunction are used to express a single complex idea that would conventionally be expressed as a noun modified by another word. It persists through literary composition, rhetorical training, and linguistic analysis as a recognized figure of speech.

A human-made pedagogical strategy: distributing study sessions over time rather than massing them. Created by cognitive scientists to exploit the psychological spacing effect; persists through curriculum design, scheduling algorithms, and educational practice.

A method of argumentation in which a proposition is assumed and shown to lead to absurdity or contradiction, thereby disproving it. Human-made logical technique, built to persist through mathematical proof, philosophical dialectic, and formal reasoning disciplines.

A rhetorical figure combining two contradictory terms to produce a new meaning, such as 'deafening silence' or 'bittersweet'. Human-made as a deliberate linguistic construct used in poetry, prose, and everyday speech to convey complex emotional states through apparent contradiction.

A concept from ancient Greek philosophy and Christian theology denoting a fundamental change of mind, heart, or way of thinking — a deep cognitive and moral transformation. Human-made as a conceptual category: the Greeks (and later the church fathers) created the term to map a specific kind of inner turning, distinguishing it from mere opinion change or emotional shift. The concept persists through philosophical discourse, theological teaching, and modern psychological literature on transformative learning.

Prompting is a human-made instructional technique: the deliberate provision of cues, questions, or hints to elicit a desired response or guide thinking. It is a structured pedagogical tool, not a natural mental process.

The human-made act of drawing a conceptual or operational boundary between things — creating difference where none was recognized. Persists through language, classification systems, categories, and cognitive habit. Not the natural things being separated, but the made act of separation itself.

The human-made analytical concept of a sign that points to its object through a causal, spatial, or temporal connection — not resemblance or convention, but direct physical linkage. Built to persist through language, logic, and semiotic analysis.
human-made rhetorical device of deliberate exaggeration beyond literal truth, deployed for emphasis, humor, or dramatic effect; persists through language, literary tradition, and social communication

A cue is a human-made concept in cognitive science and learning theory — a signal or stimulus designed or learned to guide attention, trigger memory retrieval, or initiate a response. It is an institutionalized mechanism for reducing uncertainty and directing cognition, persisting through teaching, design, and cultural transmission.

human-made act of determining the quantity of items in a set through systematic one-by-one correspondence; persists via language (number words, numerals), mathematical practice, and the cognitive habit of pairing items with ordinal positions

Doubt is the human-made map of uncertainty toward propositions — the capacity to hold a proposition without full assent, to weigh evidence against belief, to suspend judgment. It is not the natural feeling of uncertainty but the conceptual category humans built to distinguish between believing and not believing, to articulate partial certainty, and to institutionalize epistemic caution in methods like Cartesian doubt or the scientific method.

The franchise is a human-made legal-commercial arrangement in which a grantor licenses a brand, operating system, and supply chain to an independent operator in exchange for fees and ongoing compliance. It is built to persist through contract law, trademark registration, and standardized operational documentation.
human-made rhetorical device for drawing attention to something by explicitly claiming to omit or pass over it; persists through language, rhetorical teaching, and cultural practice

A human-made concept for how certain stimuli, ideas, or properties rise above the background of competing information to capture attention. The map, not the raw perceptual phenomenon — a category used across psychology, design, art, and media to describe and engineer prominence.
Human-made act of formally renouncing or rejecting a claim, affiliation, oath, or belief; persists via legal ritual, religious ceremony, and language as a speech-act category

A human-made conceptual framework for identifying paradoxical communication patterns where conflicting messages make coherent response impossible — invented by Bateson et al. at the Mental Research Institute, persisted through clinical practice, teaching, and discourse in systems theory and communication studies.

human-made concept asserting that distinct elements combine in mutually enhancing ways that transcend mere addition; persists through language, scientific discourse, and institutional reasoning across disciplines from physics to economics

A category-error is a human-made concept from philosophy (originating with Russell) naming the mistake of attributing a property to an entity that falls outside the logical category to which the property properly belongs. It is a map of a specific kind of conceptual mistake, not the natural cognition itself. The construct persists through philosophical discourse, logic education, and analytical practice as a diagnostic tool for identifying formal vs material reasoning failures.

Belief-updating is a human-constructed framework from epistemology and cognitive science naming the deliberate processes and rules by which agents revise their confidence in propositions when presented with new evidence. It is a map of reasoning practice — not the natural cognitive adjustment itself. The construct persists through formal education (Bayesian reasoning), scientific methodology, and decision theory as an explicit method for improving accuracy of belief.

Loss aversion is a human-made behavioral economics concept — the asymmetry between the psychological weight of losses and gains. Formalized by Tversky and Kahneman as part of prospect theory. The map of an asymmetric valuation function, not the natural feeling itself.
human practice of assigning words or symbols to things, concepts, or roles; persists via language, social convention, and institutional authority

The worked-example-effect is a human-made pedagogical technique — a structured learning protocol where novices study solved problems before attempting them independently. It is an institutionalized instructional method developed through educational research, designed to reduce cognitive load and build schemas in expertise development. Built to persist through teaching practices and curriculum design.
human-made act of adopting another's point of view as a deliberate cognitive practice; built to persist through language, social learning, and disciplines like psychology and diplomacy

A human-made cognitive psychology construct: the empirically measured phenomenon where actively producing information (writing, speaking, solving) yields better long-term recall than passively reading the same material. Named, operationalized, and studied in experimental labs since the 1970s; persists through teaching, research literature, and educational practice.

human-made system of classification produced by collective tagging and labeling by a community, rather than by expert taxonomy; built to persist through language practices, social platforms, and digital organization

A learning phenomenon constructed by educational psychology: the finding that the act of taking a test on material produces a lasting retention boost beyond restudying it. Human-made through experimental method, operationalised as a reproducible effect size across thousands of laboratory and classroom studies.

human-constructed practice of converting signals, data, or energy from one form to another while preserving informational content; built across technology (sensors/converters), linguistics (class-change word formation), and cognitive science (stimulus-to-encoding); persists via engineering practice, technical language, and mathematical formalism

human-constructed formal practice of defining or generating a structure by repeated application of a rule where each iteration references a prior instance; persists via mathematics (induction, fixed-point theory), computer science (recursive algorithms), and linguistic theory (recursive grammar rules)

The human-made practice of assigning names, categories, or descriptors to phenomena — a fundamental act of map-making that structures perception, enables communication, and creates the conceptual scaffolding for all higher cognition

A concept map is a human-made visual representation of knowledge structure, consisting of nodes (concepts) and labeled connecting arcs (propositions). It is an epistemic tool designed to externalize, organize, and communicate the relationships between ideas — built by education researchers (Novak et al.) to model how people organize knowledge.

a human-made cognitive concept describing the systematic error where people disregard general statistical frequencies in favor of case-specific information; built to persist through psychology curricula, decision-science literature, and behavioral-economics teaching

The human practice of naming places — assigning proper names to geographic features, settlements, and territories. It is a cultural institution that persists through language transmission, cartographic convention, and legal/territorial authority.

A human-made temporal structure that organizes activities, events, or tasks into ordered sequences over time. Created by calendars, timetables, agendas, and programs — it persists through institutional planning, personal time-management, and coordinated social action, built to extend human foresight and coordination into the future.

A human-made symbolic construct: a compact notation expressing a relationship between quantities, concepts, or operations. Formulas are outputs of formalized human reasoning — mathematics, chemistry, logic — designed to encode patterns that persist across contexts and enable calculation, prediction, and communication without restating the underlying derivation each time.
a curated collection of skills, techniques, or works held by a person or group and drawn upon through practice and teaching; built to persist via training, performance, and institutional memory
A phrase translated word-for-word from one language into another — it is human-made linguistic borrowing that persists through language contact, translation practice, and bilingual communities

the practice of converting spoken language into written form; human-made through literacy, writing systems, and phonetic notation conventions; persists via education, editorial standards, and the infrastructure of written record-keeping

A human-made reference book or card set that encodes a practical identification system — keyed visual, textual, or sensory descriptors organized to help users distinguish species, objects, or phenomena in the field; persists via publishing, teaching, and the habit of carrying it into natural or urban environments.

A value proposition is a human-made claim or framework that articulates why something is worth choosing — it is the structured articulation of benefits, differentiators, and relevance targeted at a specific audience. It exists only as a crafted communicative act: written, spoken, or designed by humans to persuade and align decisions. It persists through language, documents, and the teaching of business and marketing disciplines.

Concrete-examples is a human-made instructional technique that uses specific, tangible instances to teach abstract concepts. It is a pedagogical map — a structured method built by educators and cognitive scientists — that persists through teaching materials, lesson plans, and training curricula.

human-made cognitive techniques deliberately constructed to enhance memory encoding, storage, and retrieval. They are learned strategies — not natural faculties — that persist through teaching, cultural transmission, and deliberate practice across generations.

human-made structures for storing, organizing, and retrieving structured knowledge — from library catalogs and encyclopedias to digital databases. Built to persist beyond individual memory through systematic classification and indexing.

Indexing is the human-made practice of creating systematic lists that map topics, names, or concepts to their locations within texts or collections. It is a cognitive technology built to organize information for retrieval — constructed through deliberate cataloguing, standardized under controlled vocabularies, and persisted through publication of indexes in books, databases, and digital systems.

Schemata are human-made cognitive frameworks — structured categories of knowledge that organize information for storage and retrieval. They are the maps humans built to classify experience, built through teaching, research, and cultural transmission. The concept itself is human-made: the word, the theory, and the taxonomy of schema types (script, frame, stereotype) are all artifacts of cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

A structured pedagogical technique where learners generate and answer questions about material they are studying. Human-made as a deliberate learning strategy, built to persist through educational practice, assessment design, and the teaching of metacognitive skills.

A human-made educational construct: the concept and practice of applying learned knowledge or skills from one context to a different one. Built to persist through teaching, research, and pedagogical design.

A published list of corrections for errors identified after a work has been printed or distributed. Human-made: it is an editorial artifact, produced by authors, editors, or publishers to maintain the accuracy and integrity of published works.

A construct in educational psychology describing the process by which learners set goals, monitor their progress, and adjust strategies — human-made, taught in pedagogy programs, and persisted through curricula, assessment frameworks, and learning analytics.

A human-made concept in educational and cognitive psychology: intentionally designed mental procedures for encoding, organizing, retrieving, or evaluating information. The concept persists through academic literature, teaching practice, and the institutional frameworks of education that propagate and refine it.

A human-made learning technique where study or practice sessions are intentionally distributed over time, built to persist through instructional design and cognitive science research that demonstrates its superiority over massed practice for long-term retention
