Premeditation is a human-made cognitive practice: the deliberate advance consideration of future actions and their consequences. Built to persist through working memory, planning, and the capacity to simulate futures before acting.

Anaphora is a rhetorical device in which a word or phrase is deliberately repeated at the beginning of successive clauses, sentences, or lines. It is human-made: a conscious technique of composition, cultivated in oratory and poetry since antiquity, designed to create rhythm, emphasis, and emotional force. It persists through teaching (rhetorical handbooks), practice (speechwriting and composition), and cultural transmission across languages and genres.

A human institution in which a person or object is believed to serve as a medium for divine communication, producing prophecies or guidance through interpreted signs, speech, or text. The oracle is the constructed role and practice, not any purported supernatural source.

The practiced art of winning attraction, favor, or compliance through calculated charm, persuasion, and psychological strategy — a human technique for influencing desire and attention, distinct from any natural impulse.

Prophecy is a human-made religious institution and communicative practice — the concept of receiving, claiming, and transmitting predicted or revealed knowledge believed to originate from divine or supernatural sources. It is the MAP of future-told knowledge, not the future itself.

A problem-solving paradigm where solutions are valid only by meeting defined constraints. Human-made as a formal framework originating in operations research and AI, persisted through textbooks, algorithms, and computational practice. The map of constraint-satisfaction is the concept of framing problems as constraint sets with solution criteria.

Implicature is the human-made pragmatic concept — originating in Gricean philosophy of language — for meaning that is suggested or implied without being explicitly stated. It is the map of the gap between literal utterance and communicated intent, built to persist through teaching, analysis, and the shared conventions of conversation.

Script-knowledge is a human-made cognitive concept: a structured framework for organizing expectations about typical event sequences in familiar situations (e.g., dining at a restaurant, attending a lecture). It specifies roles, props, and ordered action sequences. The entry names the MAP — the conceptual category humans built to model predictable social sequences — not the natural cognitive processes themselves.

Noticing is the cognitive threshold event where a stimulus or pattern crosses from background processing into focal awareness. It is human-made: a concept in cognitive science (Schön's noticing), phenomenology, and education theory, describing how humans detect what warrants further attention. The map persists through teaching, scientific discipline, and everyday language distinguishing noticing from mere perception or attention.

Plausibility is the human-made concept of evaluating how believable or reasonable a claim, story, or model appears to be. It is a tool of epistemic judgment used in science, law, everyday reasoning, and risk assessment — persisting through language, argumentation norms, and cultural transmission of what counts as plausible.

A system of socially prescribed behavioral rules governing polite conduct within specific social frames — ceremonies, institutions, professions. Purely human-made; it exists only through collective agreement, teaching, and enforcement.

A human-made institutional artifact: the introductory section of a legal or foundational document (constitution, treaty, statute, charter) that states its purpose, guiding principles, and foundational context. Created by human authors for the purpose of framing the document's intent and authority. Persists through formal enactment, canonical transcription, and repeated citation.
The human-made concept of assigning proper names to geographical locations — a cartographic and linguistic practice that converts places into stable references.

The human-made system of ordering events along a temporal axis — a constructed framework of sequences, eras, and calendars that lets humans arrange happenings into readable order. Built to persist through notation, calendrical institutions, and teaching across generations.

A tally is a human-made counting method — discrete marks (strokes, notches, or tokens) made to record quantities. Created by humans to extend numerical memory beyond finger-counting, it persists through the physical substrate (wood, paper, clay) that bears the marks. One of the oldest record-keeping practices, predating written numerals.

A socially constructed claim — the map of what an agent believes or is granted they have a right to receive, hold, or do. Named by humans, deployed in law, negotiation, psychology, and social conflict. The natural referent (sense of deservingness) is out of scope; this entry covers the taxonomy and institutions that define, dispute, and enforce entitlements.

A digital public-key certificate that uses post-quantum cryptographic algorithms instead of classical ones (RSA, ECC). It is a human-made institutional artifact — defined by standards bodies (IETF, NIST), deployed by PKI infrastructure, and persists through protocol specifications, certificate authorities, and verification tooling.
A checksum is a human-made verification construct — a compact representation of data used to detect accidental or intentional corruption. It is the map of data integrity, not data itself.

A human-made navigational tool: a systematic, alphabetized listing of all words used in a text or corpus, with references to their locations. Built to persist through printed volumes, databases, and digital indices. Created by scribes, scholars, and information professionals to enable retrieval and analysis of textual content.

precedence is a human-made concept for establishing priority ordering among entities. It is produced by institutional practice — law, logic, computing, and protocol design — and persists through formal documentation, rule systems, and taught conventions. Without human agreement and recording, no priority ordering exists.
The allocation of responsibility, obligation, or weight — a human-made convention for distributing effort, proof, or care across agents. Exists through language, law, and social practice.

The human-made practice of organizing actions, events, or resources across a time reference to produce a schedule — a structured allocation of when things happen. Distinct from the schedule artifact; it is the ongoing activity of arrangement and sequencing.
The systematic practice and study of teaching methods — a human-constructed framework for how knowledge is deliberately structured and conveyed, not the natural act of learning or teaching itself
The structured set of reasons constructed to justify a decision, action, or belief. Human-made: it is a communicated, maintained, and sometimes hidden artifact of reasoning, not the reasoning itself.

The practice of systematically identifying, isolating, and correcting faults in human-made systems — software, machinery, or procedures. Debugging is a method of inquiry into broken artifacts, driven by the human-made expectation that artifacts should behave as designed.

An atlas is a human-made compilation of maps, charts, or systematic visual records organized by theme or region. It is made all the way down (Law 3): the concept of assembling a bound or indexed collection of spatial or thematic representations does not exist in nature — it requires cartographic practice, printing or digital production, editorial selection, and binding. The atlas persists through reproduction, citation, and the institutional habit of consulting it.
A terminology is a human-made system of terms with assigned meanings, built to persist across speakers within a discipline or community.

Escrow is a human-made legal and financial arrangement in which a third party holds assets, funds, or documents on behalf of two other parties until specified conditions are met. It is a constructed institution of trust, persisting through contractual agreements, standardized procedures, and institutional enforcement — not a natural phenomenon but a human solution to the problem of asymmetric risk in exchange.
A human-made plan for organizing learning content, sequences, and assessments into a coherent program. Built to persist through institutional design, written standards, and pedagogical tradition.

Liability is a human-made legal and moral construct assigning responsibility for harm, loss, or obligation. It exists in law, contracts, social norms, and institutional frameworks — pure made-side, persisting through codification, adjudication, and social enforcement.

A psychological construct developed by Albert Bandura representing the belief in one's capacity to execute behaviors necessary to produce specific performance outcomes. Entirely human-made: a theoretical framework used in education, clinical psychology, and organizational behavior to predict and influence motivation and resilience.

rent-seeking is a human-made economic concept describing the act of seeking to increase one's share of existing wealth without creating new wealth — through lobbying, regulatory capture, monopolistic practices, or other manipulations of the economic and political environment. It is a map of institutional behavior, not a natural phenomenon.

A legal-institutional role defined by law and custom in which one party is obligated to act in the best interest of another. Human-made through legal systems, contract law, and institutional practice.

A taxonomy-of-tasks is a human-made classification system that groups activities by their required skills, cognitive demands, and output types. It is built to persist through shared vocabularies in education, labor economics, and workflow design.

The human-made construct for judging probability by similarity to a prototype — a map of how people categorize, not the natural act of categorizing itself. Built to persist through teaching, naming, and disciplinary use.
A human-made epistemic and legal construct for providing grounds that support a claim, decision, or belief. It persists through language, reasoning practices, and institutional procedures.

A deliberate cognitive practice of examining one's own thoughts, actions, or knowledge. Human-made: the method and discipline of structured self-examination is a learned technique, not a spontaneous mental event.

The human-made framework for attributing mental states — beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions — to oneself and others. Not the natural capacity for empathy (that is territory), but the conceptual map: the categories, rules, and theories humans invented to predict and explain behaviour by positing inner states. Persists through language, teaching, and cultural transmission.

A human-made calibration principle used across law, ethics, and institutional practice to match the magnitude of responses, sanctions, or classifications to the gravity of their cause. Persisted through codification, teaching, and institutional reasoning.

A human-made cognitive category distinguishing types of long-term memory. The distinction between procedural (skill/habit) and declarative (fact/event) memory was coined by psychologists to map functional differences in how humans retain and reproduce learned behaviors. Per Law 2a, the entry denotes the MAP — the conceptual framework — not the natural neural mechanism.

A human-made mechanism for detecting and fixing mistakes in information systems, protocols, and processes. Built to persist through algorithms, procedures, and institutional practices that encode the distinction between correct and incorrect states.

The human-made theoretical framework in cognitive science positing two distinct modes of thinking — fast, automatic, intuitive processing and slow, deliberate, analytical processing. Built to persist through decades of experimental research, textbooks, and peer-reviewed literature as the dominant explanatory model for human judgment and decision-making.

A script is a human-made cognitive framework for organizing expected sequences of events in familiar situations. It is not the events themselves but the map — the structured expectation — that humans construct through culture, teaching, and repeated experience to predict and guide behavior in recurrent scenarios.

The default-effect is the human-made concept describing how people disproportionately prefer options that are pre-selected as the status quo. Humans built this as a category in behavioral economics and choice-architecture research to explain systematic preference for defaults, and it persists through academic literature, policy frameworks, and commercial design practices.

A human-made institutional practice of systematic investigation and verification before undertaking an obligation or transaction. Built to persist through professional standards, legal frameworks, and corporate governance protocols.

Expertise is a human-made concept denoting deeply developed competence in a domain, built through deliberate practice, accumulated experience, and structured reflection. It is a category humans use to distinguish those who can perform reliably and adaptively from novices — a distinction that organizes training, hiring, mentorship, and social status.

Human-made theoretical framework that models human cognition as operating via two distinct systems: System 1 (fast, automatic, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, effortful, analytical). Built to persist through academic teaching, research literature, and formal models in cognitive psychology and behavioral economics.

Negligence is a human-made legal construct: the failure to exercise the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would exercise in like circumstances. Built through centuries of common law to assign liability for harm caused by carelessness, it persists as a category in tort law across jurisdictions worldwide.

A meme is a human-made concept for a unit of cultural information — a pattern, idea, behavior, or style that spreads from person to person within a culture through imitation and communication. The concept itself was coined by Richard Dawkins in 'The Selfish Gene' (1976) as a framework for understanding cultural evolution. It is made by human cognition and language, designed to persist across minds through replication.

Gamification is a human-made practice — the deliberate application of game-design elements (points, badges, leaderboards, challenges, progress feedback) to non-game contexts (education, workplace, health, marketing) to motivate participation and shape behavior. It did not exist before humans invented it in the late 2000s as a named design practice.

A human-made legal construct: the deposit of money, property, or security as guarantee for the performance of an obligation or the fulfillment of a condition. Built to persist through statutes, contracts, and institutional practice across jurisdictions.

a human-made figure of speech in which words are used to mean the opposite of their literal sense, typically for humor, irony, or criticism; built to persist through literary tradition, social practice, and the shared conventions of pragmatic language use

A pun is a human-made linguistic construct — a deliberate exploitation of word ambiguity, homophony, or double meaning for humorous or rhetorical effect. It is a map (the concept of wordplay), not the natural thing. Humans invented puns as a form of linguistic play, and they persist through teaching and cultural transmission.

A human-made conceptual framework for describing path-dependence: the phenomenon where a system's current state depends on its history, not just its present inputs. The concept of hysteresis — borrowed from physics, adopted across economics, materials science, psychology — is a map of a pattern, not the pattern itself. The word and the analytical category are human inventions used to track lag, memory, and irreversibility in modeled systems.

a human-made pedagogical construct — a method of instruction organized as question-and-answer for systematic teaching and memorization, developed in religious traditions and extended to secular domains

The human-made concept of threshold states — the quality of being betwixt and between established categories, roles, or phases. Coined by anthropologist Arnold van Gennep to describe rites of passage and expanded by Victor Turner. A conceptual framework humans built to identify and analyze transitional periods in ritual, social structure, and personal development. Built to persist through language, anthropological theory, and cultural analysis.

Docket is a human made legal administrative construct the formal record and schedule of cases assigned to be heard by a court or tribunal. Built to persist through institutional record keeping and procedural law governing judicial administration.

Footwear is a human-made category of protective garments designed to cover and shield the feet. It is an institution of material culture that persists through manufacturing traditions, design conventions, and social norms about appropriate dress. Every pair of shoes, boots, sandals, or socks is an instance of this human-made construct — the natural foot is not footwear; the category and the things made to fill it are.

Human-made method and concept of examining one's own conscious experience. Rooted in philosophy (Descartes' methodic doubt), adopted as experimental psychology (Wundt), and preserved across contemplative traditions. The concept itself is human-made; per Law 2a, the entry denotes the map.

The human-made virtue and epistemological framework of recognizing the limits of one's knowledge. It is not the natural state of ignorance — it is the cultivated disposition, taught through philosophy and discourse, to acknowledge what one does not know.

Intention is a human-made concept — the cognitive framework for representing goals, purposes, and planned actions. Every culture builds maps of intent to coordinate collective action, assign responsibility, and distinguish accident from design. It persists through language, law, and social practice.

The human-constructed category for conscious recognition — the map humans drew to pick out and discuss the phenomenon of being-alive-to-one-s-situation, self, or world. A construct, not the natural phenomenon.

A human-made concept for systematic patterns of deviation from rationality and objectivity in the gathering and evaluation of evidence. Built to persist through cognitive science, critical pedagogy, and epistemology as a framework for diagnosing flawed reasoning in knowledge work.

A human-made collection of documents assembled about a person, subject, or event — organized for reference, surveillance, or decision. Built to persist through archiving, filing systems, and institutional memory; exists as a social and bureaucratic technology for aggregating scattered information into a single investigable object.
The conventional spelling system of a language — a human-made set of rules for representing sounds as written symbols. Built to persist through education, publishing, and institutional enforcement.

The human-made practice of reanalyzing unfamiliar words to fit familiar patterns — a cognitive mechanism for word-formation that produces shared folk explanations for word origins (like possum from possumum, or peahen from pever). It is a human-made conceptual process, not a natural phenomenon.

A human-made linguistic concept: the original word or morpheme from which another word or form is derived. Etymons are identified through comparative and historical linguistics as the reconstructed sources of modern words. They persist as scholarly constructs in dictionaries, etymological databases, and linguistic teaching. Law 2a: etymons denote the map — the reconstructed ancestral forms posited by linguistic science, not the natural sounds themselves.

A human-made structured set of interrelated concepts, categories, and relationships used to organize thinking and inquiry within a domain. Built through writing, teaching, and institutional practice to persist across time.

Totemism is a human-made system of social organization and symbolic identity — a cultural framework in which groups (clans, lineages, tribes) adopt specific animals, plants, or natural objects as markers of kinship, territory, and collective identity. It is a constructed social taxonomy, not a natural classification.

Memetics is a human-made theoretical framework for studying how cultural information — ideas, behaviors, styles — replicates, mutates, and spreads through populations. It is the map of cultural transmission, not the natural spread itself. The self is an entry; the human-animal is not. Memetics maps the patterns of cultural inheritance.
a psychological framework developed by German psychologists in the early 20th century that posits human perception organizes sensory input into unified wholes rather than isolated elements

The human practice of organizing entities into structured categories — hierarchical or networked — based on shared properties, purposes, or conventions. It is a cognitive and social technology for taming complexity, not a natural phenomenon.

The social practice of using formal credentials — degrees, certifications, titles — as the primary marker of competence, authority, and legitimacy. Human-made: it is an institution of social evaluation, built and maintained by educational and professional systems that assign status based on demonstrated (or purchased) qualifications rather than direct evidence of ability.

The concept of imitation or representation as a cultural and artistic principle. Human-made since antiquity — debated by Plato, Aristotle, and subsequent philosophy of art. Persists through discourse in aesthetics, literary theory, and cultural studies as a framework for understanding how art represents reality.

The vernacular is a human-made linguistic construct — the everyday language or dialect of ordinary people within a community. It is an output of human social making: communities produce and maintain vernaculars through practice, transmission, and boundary-drawing against formal or literary registers. It persists through spoken/written use and cultural reproduction.

iconicity is the human-made concept of a sign's resemblance to its referent — the property by which words, gestures, or symbols evoke the thing they denote through shared form or structure. It is a map-concept in semiotic theory, used to classify and reason about how signs work. Built to persist through teaching, linguistic analysis, and artistic practice.

A philosophical construct from epistemology — the set of intellectual character traits (open-mindedness, intellectual humility, intellectual courage, thoroughness) that enable reliable knowledge acquisition and reasoning. Human-made: coined and developed within the philosophical tradition from Aristotle through modern epistemology, taught and debated in academic disciplines.

Deliberation is a human-made practice of systematically weighing options, evidence, and consequences before making a decision. It is not a natural impulse but a structured cognitive activity — councils, committees, judicial processes, decision matrices — that persists through institutional design, written procedures, and teaching.
the human-made concept of using signs, symbols, or words to point to something else — a foundational mechanism of meaning-making in language, cognition, and communication

The prototype is a human-made conceptual model for categorization: the idea that categories are organized around typical examples rather than strict definitions. It is an output of cognitive science, a map built to explain how humans actually group things, not the natural phenomenon of similarity itself.

A human-made argumentative technique: the deliberate misrepresentation of an opponent's position — exaggeration, distortion, or fabrication — to create a weakened target that is easier to attack. Built to persist through rhetorical education, debate practice, and logical analysis as a named fallacy category.

A human-made epistemological concept naming situations where two things cannot be compared because they lack a common measure. Built to persist through academic discourse, paradigm disputes, and cross-cultural analysis.

A human-made rhetorical and literary device: the act of anticipating an objection or future event and addressing it before it arises. Built to persist through teaching in rhetoric, composition, and literary theory.

Accounting is a human-made system for recording, classifying, summarizing, and interpreting economic transactions. It is the map of value flows — not the wealth itself, but the constructed practice of quantifying and making accountable what humans produce and exchange. Built to persist through standardized categories (debtor/creditor, asset/liability, revenue/expense), double-entry structures, and periodic reporting cycles that enable comparison across time.

The practice of translating abstract concepts into observable, measurable indicators — a human-made method for making the theoretical tractable in research, law, medicine, and science. Built to persist through protocols, instruments, and institutional validation.

A human-made legal and ethical obligation arising from fiduciary relationships, where one party is required to act in the best interest of another. It is a formalized construct of trust-law that structures decision-making authority and loyalty in professional, commercial, and institutional contexts.
a systematic approach to inquiry and practice, built by humans to structure how knowledge is produced and problems are solved

vigilance is the human-constructed practice of maintaining careful, sustained observation — institutionalized in security protocols, medical monitoring, and quality assurance. It is not the natural faculty of alertness but the organized, rule-governed form of watching for threats or deviations.

A human-made principle for determining which facts, errors, or items are significant enough to influence decisions, judgments, or reporting. Built to persist through professional standards (accounting GAAP/IFRS), legal precedent, institutional policy, and pedagogical transmission.
human-made psychological and contemplative practice of focused present-moment awareness, formalized in Eastern traditions and Western clinical psychology

Human-made concept for measuring logical consistency among propositions, perceptual unity among elements, and systemic compatibility. Built to persist through formal systems, scientific method, and cross-disciplinary theory-building. The map of how parts hang together, not the natural state of things.

A human-made organizational concept from Science and Technology Studies — an entity that enables cooperation between distinct social worlds (disciplines, professions, communities) while remaining flexible enough to adapt to local needs and constraints. Built to persist through institutional design, organizational practice, and the material artifacts that mediate between groups.

A human-made psychological construct: the shared system by which groups encode, store, and retrieve knowledge across members — each person knows not just content but who knows what. Born from social cognition research, it persists through language, teaching, and institutional practice.
The human-made construct of the faculty of conscious choice — a concept from philosophy and psychology describing how agents represent and exercise deliberate decision-making

Human-made practice of remote measurement and data transmission: the systematic collection of operational data from distant or inaccessible sources, transmitted for monitoring, analysis, and control. Built to persist through standardized protocols, storage infrastructure, and dashboards that convert raw signals into actionable information.

The cognitive process of organizing and interpreting sensory information into meaningful patterns. Human-made in that the very concept of 'perception' as a distinct mental faculty is a theoretical construct developed through philosophy, psychology, and cognitive science — it is the map of how we pick out regularities from sensory input, not the raw neural firing itself.

The narrative framework of a culture or worldview — the story-structure humans construct to give meaning, identity, and purpose to collective existence. Built to persist through mythopoetic practice, ritual retelling, and cultural transmission across generations.

The human-made practice of imbuing actions, objects, or spaces with ritual significance — a social and cultural process that transforms ordinary activities into meaningful, structured practices through symbolic assignment and collective agreement.

The concept of epistemic vigilance — a framework humans built to categorize and manage the cognitive mechanisms for evaluating the reliability of others' claims, testimony, and information. It is a made map for navigating trust, credibility, and source-evaluation in social knowledge exchange.

The practice of selectively obscuring, editing, or removing content from documents and records — a human-made procedure used in law, journalism, administration, and security. Built to persist through institutional protocols (classification systems, legal requirements, editorial standards) and encoded in the persistent artifacts that emerge from it.

The concept of texts referencing, echoing, and drawing meaning from other texts — a human-made theoretical framework for analyzing how writing and discourse operate as woven networks of citation, allusion, quotation, and pastiche rather than isolated artifacts.

the human-constructed practice of self-referential examination — systems, institutions, and discourses that turn back upon themselves to monitor, evaluate, and modify their own operation. Persisted through social theory, scientific methodology, organizational governance, and everyday sensemaking.

human-made theory of cognition: the concept that knowledge is not represented internally but enacted through dynamic interaction between agent and environment; built by Varela, Thompson, and Rosch to replace computationalist models

a human-made theory of cognition proposing that meaning emerges through the selective integration of mental content from separate conceptual spaces, built to persist through linguistic theory, cognitive science pedagogy, and creative practice

A human-made concept in epistemology and social philosophy that classifies systematic harms done to others in their capacity as knowers — testimonial injustice, hermeneutical injustice, and structural forms thereof. Built to persist through academic disciplines, feminist philosophy, and applied ethics.

Teleology is a human-made explanatory framework: the practice of accounting for phenomena by their purpose, goal, or end-state (final cause) rather than by antecedent or efficient causes. Built to persist because it structures inquiry across philosophy, biology, ethics, and design — from Aristotelian final causes through Darwinian functional explanation to modern AI goal-directed systems.

Distanciation is a human-made conceptual framework from hermeneutic philosophy (Ricoeur) describing how acts, norms, and texts become detached from their originating agents and contexts, acquiring autonomous trajectories of meaning and persistence. It is a map of the severance between intention and effect that every human creation undergoes — not the natural act itself but the concept that tracks how social meaning outlives its maker.

The human practice of creating systematic records — catalogs, inventories, indices — to organize and make discoverable collections of items, information, or knowledge. It is a map-construction activity: not the things gathered, but the taxonomic apparatus humans build to hold them. Persists through libraries, archives, databases, and all recording institutions.

A human-made philosophical tradition and method for describing the structures of conscious experience as they appear, without reducing them to causal explanations. Built to persist through teaching, textual transmission, and cross-disciplinary application from philosophy to psychology, sociology, and the arts.

The concept of intentionality — the capacity of mental states to be about, represent, or be directed at objects, states of affairs, or other mental states. A human-made philosophical construct arising from the study of consciousness, language, and meaning. The map, not the feeling it describes.

A human-made psychoanalytic concept describing how emotional and psychic energy invests in objects, ideas, or other people within a mental economy. The map is the concept itself — the framework Freud built to track libidinal investment — not any natural psychological faculty.

A human-made model of interpretation from hermeneutic philosophy: understanding requires a recursive movement between parts of a text and its whole meaning. The concept is a map built by philosophers (Heidegger, Gadamer) to describe how interpretation iterates — not the cognitive mechanism itself, but the theoretical framework for analyzing interpretive practice.

the human practice of preserving records, artifacts, and knowledge across time through systematic organization and storage — made possible by institutions, conventions, and technologies of preservation

Affect is a human-made concept denoting pre-personal, pre-cognitive intensity of feeling — the raw force of sensation before it is organized into named emotions. Originating in Spinoza's conatus and developed through Deleuze, Massumi, and affect theory, it is a map carved by philosophers and psychologists to distinguish raw intensity from structured emotion. Built to persist through theoretical discourse, clinical practice, and cultural analysis.

Qualia is a human-made philosophical concept denoting the subjective, qualitative character of conscious experience — what it feels like to see red, taste coffee, or feel pain. Coined in analytical philosophy of mind (C.I. Lewis, later popularized by Frank Jackson's knowledge argument), it is a map built to categorize the felt character of experience distinct from its functional or physical description. Built to persist through philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and phenomenology.

Problematization is a human-made theoretical concept in philosophy (especially Foucault), social theory, and public policy that denotes the discursive practice of framing an condition, phenomenon, or situation as a 'problem' requiring intervention, analysis, or solution. The concept was systematized by Foucault to describe how regimes of truth produce objects of knowledge by converting phenomena into problem-objects. The map of a concept — not the natural condition itself.

human-made theoretical concept describing the system of embodied dispositions, inclinations, and practical schemas that people acquire through social experience and that generate practices and perceptions. It is the map of how social structures become second nature — a human invention in social theory, not a natural faculty.

defamiliarization is the human-made artistic technique of presenting familiar subjects in an unfamiliar or strange way, thereby disrupting automatic perception and forcing renewed attention. Originating in Russian Formalism (Shklovsky's ostranenie), it is a constructed method — not a natural cognitive state — designed to break habitual reading and restore the sensation of experience. It persists through deliberate craft, taught as a technique in literature, art, and film.

reduction is a human-made epistemological concept — the strategy of explaining one phenomenon by mapping it to another, more fundamental domain. It exists as a methodological principle across philosophy and the sciences, persisting through academic discourse and pedagogical practice.

Deixis is a human-made linguistic construct: the system of context-dependent reference (here/there, now/then, I/you) encoded in language. It is a map for anchoring utterance to situation — a tool for orienting speakers and listeners in shared space, time, and personhood.

Consciousness as a concept is human-made: the category humans built to track subjective experience, self-awareness, and the distinction between mental and non-mental states. It appears across philosophical discourse (Descartes to Chalmers), psychological theory, neuroscientific investigation, and religious frameworks. The natural phenomenon of being aware is not the entry — the conceptual map of awareness is.

The conceptual framework humans built to study how symbolic representations acquire meaning through connection to the world or to other representations. It is the map — the theoretical construct — not the physical relation itself. Human-made as a research program, theoretical concept, and explanatory framework in semiotics, cognitive science, and artificial intelligence.

Hypallage is a figure of speech invented by human speakers and grammarians: the practice of attaching an adjective to a noun it does not semantically modify, displacing it from its proper grammatical anchor. It exists as a pattern of speech, a named device taught in rhetoric, and a recognizable effect in literary texts — all human-made linguistic constructs.

Teaching is the human-made institution of systematically transmitting knowledge, skills, and cultural maps across generations. It is output by human making — schools, curricula, pedagogical methods, apprenticeship models — all constructed to persist through social practice. The natural faculty of learning exists without teaching; teaching itself is the artifact.

Foregrounding is a human-made rhetorical and literary device — the deliberate amplification of certain textual features to make them stand out and disrupt automated perception. It is built to persist through literary teaching, critical discourse, and textual practice.

The human-made map-concept of emotional purification — the theoretical category developed since Aristotle for the claim that engagement with art, ritual, or narrative purges, cleanses, or transforms emotional states. Persisted through literary theory, aesthetics, psychoanalysis, and drama as a explanatory framework for why humans create and consume emotionally powerful works.

Prosody is the human-constructed concept of rhythmic structure in speech — the systematic study and categorization of stress, intonation, rhythm, and syllable patterns as a dimension of linguistic analysis. It is a scholarly framework built to describe and classify how spoken language carries meaning through non-segmental features.

Allusion is a human-made rhetorical and literary construct — the concept of indirect reference that allows a text to invoke something else without naming it directly. It is a map built by humans to categorize a pattern of communication where meaning is carried by implication rather than statement. The natural side would be the psychological act of remembering, but the entry names the conceptual framework that makes allusion possible as a recognized technique across literature, rhetoric, and everyday discourse.

Symbolism is a human-made system of signs where concrete objects, actions, or forms stand for abstract ideas, qualities, or principles beyond their literal meaning. It is a cultural technology for encoding meaning — built through convention, taught across generations, and sustained by shared interpretive practice. Without symbolic interpretation, the sign remains inert.

Didactics is a human-made systematic discipline that studies and theorizes the methods, principles, and practices of teaching. It is an academic construct produced by educational scholars, structured through scholarly discourse and teacher training programs, designed to persist across generations of pedagogical refinement.

The concept that the body is not merely a vessel for mind but the medium through which experience, cognition, and meaning arise. A theoretical framework developed in philosophy, cognitive science, and cultural theory that treats bodily existence as constitutive of knowing and meaning-making, not incidental to it.

Indexicality is the linguistic and semiotic concept that certain signs (words like 'I', 'here', 'now') derive their reference from the context of their own use. It is a human-made conceptual category used in linguistics, philosophy of language, and semiotics to explain how language anchors meaning to situational context — not the contextual relation itself, but the concept of how that anchoring works.

A theoretical framework in cognitive science and philosophy of mind that posits cognition is not confined to brain computation but is constitutively shaped by the body's structure, sensorimotor capacities, and real-time interactions with the environment. Human-made as a formal research programme originating in the 1990s (Varela, Thompson, Rosch; Clark; Lakoff & Johnson) and sustained through peer-reviewed literature, conferences, and institutional funding.

metacognition is the human-made concept of reflecting on and monitoring one's own cognitive processes — a framework developed in psychology and cognitive science to study self-aware thought. It is not the natural faculty of introspection but the constructed category that picks out meta-level cognitive operations.

Packaging is a human-made practice of designing and producing containers, wrappers, and protective systems for goods. It is an output of industrial and commercial making — not a natural phenomenon. The practice persists through trade, logistics, and consumer culture, structured by material engineering and marketing conventions.

Hypernym is a human-made linguistic concept — a classificatory relationship in semantics where a general term (hypernym) encompasses more specific terms (hyponyms). It is a tool of lexical analysis and categorization, not a natural category. The word 'animal' is a hypernym of 'dog'; 'furniture' is a hypernym of 'chair'. This entry names the concept itself, the map that lets us reason about lexical structure.

The concept of emergence is a human-made framework for understanding how macro-level patterns, properties, or behaviors arise from micro-level interactions — the whole exhibiting features not reducible to its parts. It is a map, not the phenomenon itself, and persists through scientific and philosophical discourse across disciplines.

Compression is a human-made information-processing technique: the systematic reduction of data size while preserving recoverable content. It is built to persist through encoded algorithms, standardized protocols, and implementation in software and hardware — a conceptual framework that exists only through human invention and maintenance.

Human-made systematic study of family descent and lineage. Built to persist through genealogical records, family trees, oral traditions, and institutional archives that maintain knowledge of ancestry across generations.

Translation is the human-made practice of rendering meaning from one language into another, preserving intent while transforming expression. Built to persist through teaching, written practice, and technological tools.

A signal is a human-made carrier of information — a deliberate pattern or variation in a medium designed to convey meaning across distance or time. Built to persist through encoding conventions, repetition, and institutionalized interpretation protocols.

Zoning is a human-made system of land use regulation where governments divide territory into zones with specific permitted uses, building types, and density limits. It persists through legal codes, enforcement mechanisms, and public records — a map of what humans have decided different places should be made for.

Standardization is a human-made regulatory and economic practice — institutions create specifications, trade agreements establish norms, and markets enforce consistency. It persists through written standards bodies (ISO, IEEE), regulatory frameworks, and the economic necessity of interoperability.
concept — the human-made idea of a continuous sequence where adjacent elements differ minimally while distant elements differ more, enabling graded transitions without sharp boundaries

Literature is a human-made category of creative and imaginative writing, sustained through language, teaching, and institutional curation — not nature itself but a classification humans built to distinguish certain written works by their aesthetic and imaginative qualities.
Human-constructed concept categorizing the universal finitude of living organisms; the condition of being subject to death as a meaningful category, not the biological event itself.

A novel is a human-made narrative form — an extended prose fiction structured as a sustained fictional world. It is an institution of literature, sustained by publishing, reading cultures, and literary tradition. The novel persists through material books, digital files, and the cultural practice of novel-reading.

An epithet is a human-made naming convention — a descriptive term or phrase attached to a proper name to highlight a characteristic quality. It persists through literary tradition, oral formulaic composition, and linguistic usage (e.g., 'Alexander the Great', 'Homer'). The epithet is a structured practice of character-attaching naming, sustained by cultural memory and textual transmission.

A role is a human-made construct: a set of expectations, behaviors, obligations, and rights attached to a specific position within a social structure, institution, or system. It is the map of what a position requires — not the person occupying it. Natural beings occupy positions; roles are the human-made scripts that define what those positions entail.
a brief narrative form that conveys a moral lesson through anthropomorphic characters or simplified scenarios, created by human storytellers and persisted through oral and written tradition

A structured ritual practice for handling the dead, involving preparation of the body, communal gathering, and symbolic transition. Human-made, not natural — every culture that has one builds its own distinct map of what death requires.

A vineyard is a human-made agricultural estate cultivated with grapevines for wine or table-grape production, organized through deliberate land preparation, trellising systems, and seasonal management — a cultural-technological practice that persists across generations.

A human-made construct: a structured set of instructions for preparing a dish, product, or outcome. Built to persist through written tradition, oral teaching, and cultural transmission across generations. The recipe is the map of repeated making, not any single instance of it.

A human-made publication: a systematic annual compilation of facts, statistics, and reference data organized by subject, produced by human editors and compilers for public reference. Built to persist through periodic publication cycles and archival reproduction.
A human-made political and military construct: the formal act of yielding under negotiated terms, distinguishing negotiated surrender from mere defeat or conquest
A pact is a human-made formal agreement between parties, a construct of law and custom designed to create binding mutual obligations and persist across time through documentation or ritual.

A systematic compilation of human knowledge organized by topic, created by authors and editors to persist and disseminate information across time. Built to endure through compilation, curation, and reproduction.

A human-made system for compiling, organizing, and presenting lists of published works and sources. It is an institutionalized practice of attribution and sourcing, built to persist through citation conventions and cataloging standards.

A systematic procedure designed to achieve a specific result through repeatable steps. Human-made: methods are constructs of human planning, designed to standardize and reproduce successful practices. Built to persist: they endure through documentation, teaching, and repeated application across time and practitioners.

A summa is a comprehensive systematic treatise on a subject — a human-made genre of organized writing that collects, structures, and presents all known knowledge on a topic in a single authoritative work.
A catalogue is a human-made systematic listing of items, organized by category or attribute, designed to persist across time as a reference tool for identification and retrieval.

The human-made concept of official forgiveness or remission of punishment granted by an authority to an offender. Pardon operates within legal and political systems as a mechanism for clemency,赦免, or amnesty.

The human-made concept of objects crafted by humans that carry cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance beyond mere utility. Artifacts are preserved, studied, and displayed as records of human activity.

The category of printed books, pamphlets, and broadsheets produced during the earliest period of European printing (before 1501 CE), and the scholarly concept used to classify this transitional form between manuscript and modern print culture. Human-made: the term, the chronological boundary, and the category itself were invented by later bibliographers to describe a specific historical production method.

Leverage is the human-made principle of using a small input to amplify an output — across mechanical, social, financial, and rhetorical domains. It names the strategy of positioning advantage to multiply effect, not the physical tool itself (lever) but the abstracted concept of multiplicative force that humans discovered and systematized.

Value is the human-made concept of worth — a scale or standard by which people judge things as good, bad, useful, beautiful, or important. It is entirely constructed through cultural agreement, economic systems, and moral frameworks; no value exists in nature without a valuer.

A cliché is a human-made linguistic construct: an expression that was once novel or effective but has lost its expressive force through excessive repetition. It exists purely within language, discourse, and communication practice — the territory of actual repeated speech is not the cliché itself; the category of 'overused expression' that speakers recognize and deploy is the construct. Persistence mechanism: language usage, social recognition, cultural memory.

Censorship is the human-made practice of suppressing, editing, or controlling the flow of information, speech, or artistic expression. It is a social and institutional mechanism — enforced through laws, norms, editorial decisions, and power structures — designed to shape what can be known, said, or seen. It persists through codified regulations, social sanctions, and the institutional authority to control channels of communication.

Rationality is a human-made framework of reasoning — constructed principles, standards, and methods for evaluating claims and making decisions. It is not the natural biological capacity for thought, but the cultural and intellectual apparatus of what counts as 'reasonable,' varying across domains (logic, science, law, practical deliberation) and epochs.

The human-made concept of being embedded in a particular context, position, or set of circumstances. It is the MAP of contextual embedding — a category used across phenomenology, sociology, and epistemology to describe how agents, knowledge, and meaning are always positioned within specific frameworks, practices, and environments. The actual circumstances are natural, but the concept of situatedness itself is human-made: it is a theoretical tool for analyzing how context shapes possibility, understanding, and action.

Vocabulary is the constructed set of words and terms that a language, discipline, or community uses to encode and communicate meaning. It is a human-made lexicon — not the natural capacity for speech, but the curated inventory of signs that persists through teaching, writing, and social use. Without the practice of language, vocabulary dissolves.

A workaround is a human-made strategy for bypassing a limitation, restriction, or failure without resolving the underlying cause. It is a creative improvisation — part technique, part knowledge — that enables continued operation when the intended path is blocked. Humans invent, share, and transmit workarounds through practice, documentation, and example; they persist as reproducible patterns of behavior.

Personification is a human-made rhetorical and cognitive device: the practice of attributing human qualities, emotions, or agency to non-human entities (animals, objects, natural forces, abstract concepts). It is a map that humans construct to make the unfamiliar legible through the familiar — clearly output by human making under Law 1, and the word itself is the construct, not any natural phenomenon.

Proverb is a human-made linguistic construct: a short, conventional saying that encodes a perceived truth or piece of advice. It is not the natural wisdom itself but the verbal form humans craft to package and transmit it — a cultural artifact built to persist across generations through language, teaching, and oral or written tradition.

The human-made concept of interpreting natural events, signs, or occurrences as predictive signals of future events — a cognitive framework for reading meaning into contingency, not the events themselves

Rumor is a human-made construct: the concept of unverified information transmitted through a community. The word names a social mechanism, not any natural phenomenon — it is a map humans built to track how claims circulate without verification.

A human-made philosophical concept: the theory that learning is recollection of pre-existing knowledge. Originating in Platonic thought, it constructs knowledge as retrieval rather than acquisition — a map-category for a specific epistemological model humans have used to explain learning, education, and the nature of the soul across philosophical traditions.
A human-made device designed to replace or augment a missing or impaired anatomical structure, preserving or restoring function through engineered materials and interfaces.

A human-made construct providing an alternative account of one's whereabouts or actions, used to disprove accusation or assign blame elsewhere. Built to persist through documentation, witness testimony, and institutional verification systems.

A human-made linguistic device that deploys words in non-literal or specially structured ways to produce rhetorical effects beyond their ordinary semantic meaning — a category of expressive construction built through language use, taught and preserved through grammar and rhetoric

A rhetorical device in which something is expressed in milder terms than warranted, deliberately downplaying significance to produce effect — human-made, language-based, used across cultures and epochs.

A linguistic device in which a word, phrase, or sequence reads identically forwards and backwards — a human-made pattern built from the conventions of writing and speech, not a property of nature itself.

A humor device in which a reference, gesture, or phrase is only funny to people who share the background knowledge required to recognize it — a human-made pattern built from the conventions of social context and shared experience, not a property of nature itself.

The concept and practice of intentionally inducing false belief through concealment or misrepresentation — a human-made category and set of techniques codified across law (fraud, perjury), strategy (military doctrine, competitive games), narrative, and social interaction. Not the natural impulse to mislead but the constructed map that classifies, teaches, and institutionalizes intentional false-belief induction.

The practice of using fallacious reasoning, presented as valid argument, to persuade — a technique of disputation and rhetoric taught in debate and refined across philosophy, law, and political discourse.

A human-made argumentative technique: a distracting element introduced into a debate or discourse to divert attention away from the relevant issue. Built to persist through teaching in rhetoric, logic, and critical discourse.

A classical Greek rhetorical concept: the opportune moment — the quality of timing that makes an argument or action effective. A map of persuasive timing, built to persist through teaching in rhetoric, philosophy, and rhetoric-criticism as a dimension of evaluation distinct from chronological measure.

A figure-of-speech is a human-made linguistic construct: a word or phrase deliberately crafted to carry two distinct meanings, one typically straightforward and the other subversive or risqué. Humans invented it to compress ambiguity into a single utterance, building social games around interpretation that persist through teaching, literature, and everyday conversation.

Prudence is a human-constructed virtue — practical wisdom that governs judgment in action. Named and classified within ethical systems across cultures, it persists through philosophical discourse, moral education, and cultural transmission.

A systematic communication campaign designed to shape public perception and elicit specific responses. Human-made technique of influence, persisting through institutional practice, media channels, and organizational apparatus.

A false dilemma is a human-made reasoning construct that misrepresents a situation by presenting exactly two alternatives when more options actually exist. It is a rhetorical and logical device used to constrain choice, force a binary decision, and eliminate nuance through artificial partitioning of possibility space.

A human-made linguistic construct: the named category of verbal error where a speaker substitutes a word with another that sounds phonetically similar but differs in meaning, conventionally producing a humorous or mistaken effect. The construct persists through etymological teaching (after Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's 1775 play), dictionary definition, and cultural literacy as a recognized type of semantic substitution error.

A human-made fallacy: the argumentative tactic of attacking the character, motive, or personal attributes of an opponent rather than addressing their argument. Built to derail reasoning by shifting focus from claims to claimants, it persists through teaching in debate, education, and critical thinking curricula.

A human-made linguistic strategy: the deliberate use of a disparaging, offensive, or pejorative term in place of a neutral or more polite alternative. Built to express contempt, hostility, or ridicule through language substitution — the functional opposite of euphemism. Persists as a recognized communicative pattern in any culture that uses loaded vocabulary to shade meaning.

A dichotomy is a human-constructed classification scheme that divides a domain into exactly two mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive categories. It is a rhetorical and logical device, built through the practice of categorization and sustained in language, mathematics, and formal reasoning as a tool for simplifying complexity into binary opposition.

A fallacy in which a key term or phrase is used with two or more different meanings within a single argument, misleadingly exploiting the ambiguity to produce a conclusion that only holds under one of those senses.

a rhetorical device that juxtaposes contrasting ideas in parallel structure to highlight their opposition — a human-made pattern of expression built to persist through language, teaching, and literary tradition
a human-made pattern of language structured to produce specific effects on an audience — built to persist through teaching, literary tradition, and cultural transmission

Bandwagon is a human-made propaganda technique that persuades by appealing to the desire to conform — 'everyone is doing it, so you should too.' Built to persist through social psychology and mass media, it manipulates the human need for belonging as a lever of influence.

A figure of speech and rhetorical device in which words, grammatical constructions, or concepts are repeated in reverse order. Human-made linguistic structure, deliberately crafted for emphasis, memorability, and persuasive effect.

A deliberate compositional technique in which two or more elements are placed side by side to produce contrast, resonance, or new meaning through their adjacency — used in visual art, literature, rhetoric, music, design, and film. Human-made by construction: it requires an agent to choose what to place beside what and why.
A logical fallacy in which the conclusion of an argument is assumed as a premise, reasoning circularly so that the point to be proved is already taken for granted in the supporting argument

A human-made pattern of reasoning that appears valid but fails to establish its conclusion — a structured error in argumentation, catalogued and classified across the disciplines of logic, rhetoric, and critical thinking

A sophism is a human-made rhetorical and logical construct: a seemingly plausible argument designed to deceive, structured to appear valid while concealing a logical flaw. It persists through language, debate, and pedagogy as a category of fallacious reasoning.

A human-made rhetorical device: a figure of speech employing deliberate understatement for emphasis, irony, or humorous effect. It persists through language use, rhetorical instruction, and literary analysis.

Human-made rhetorical device: the deliberate act of mentioning something by claiming to omit it, constructed through language and sustained by shared recognition of its ironic structure in persuasion.

Aposiopesis is a human-made rhetorical device — a deliberate figure of speech in which a sentence is abruptly broken off and left unfinished, the ending being left to the reader or listener's imagination. It is a convention of written and spoken language, used to convey overwhelming emotion, hesitation, threat, or dramatic pause, and persists through literary tradition, theatrical practice, and everyday linguistic usage.

Asyndeton is a human-made rhetorical construct: the deliberate omission of conjunctions from a series of coordinated words, phrases, or clauses to produce compression, acceleration, or emphasis. It is a technique of composition and performance, taught and analyzed within rhetoric and poetics.

A human-made rhetorical figure — the deliberate use of multiple conjunctions in close succession to create rhythm, emphasis, or a sense of abundance. Built to persist through rhetorical pedagogy, literary analysis, and stylistic practice.

A rhetorical and typographic device in which one or more words are deliberately omitted from a sentence or passage, relying on context for the reader to supply them. Human-made through the conventions of writing, editing, and literary style.

A rhetorical device in which a speaker or writer uses more words than necessary to express an idea, substituting a phrase for a simpler term — a deliberate circumlocution for stylistic, euphemistic, or emphatic effect.

A mechanical construct with few or no moving parts that multiplies or redirects force — one of the six classical simple machines (lever, wheel-and-axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw). Human-made as a classification and as individual artifacts, persisted through teaching, apprenticeship, and engineering practice.

A pleonasm is a human-made linguistic construct: the use of more words than necessary to express an idea (e.g., 'free gift', 'end result', 'past history'). It is a recognized category of redundancy in rhetoric and grammar, taught and analyzed in language disciplines as a stylistic or grammatical phenomenon.

A tautology is a human-made figure of speech and logical form in which the same proposition is expressed twice using different words — e.g. 'A is A,' 'the big giant monster,' or 'he arrived at the scene of the accident.' It is a construct of rhetoric and formal logic, created by humans to flag circularity, emphasis, or empty repetition. It persists through pedagogical teaching, logical analysis, and stylistic critique.

Eponym is a human-made naming convention by which the name of a known person, place, or established thing is transferred to a new entity — sustained by linguistic convention, cultural memory, and institutional naming practice.

A human-made concept: the identification and use of a recurring element, feature, or pattern within a creative work or across a body of work, where the recurrence carries interpretive significance beyond mere repetition. Built to persist through cultural transmission, critical analysis, and teaching across artistic disciplines.

A rhetorical figure in which a single word is applied to two others in different senses — one literal, one figurative — creating a semantic juxtaposition. It is human-made as a recognized construct of grammar and rhetoric, persisted through grammatical tradition, rhetoric textbooks, and literary analysis.

A human-made representational construct used to understand, explain, or predict aspects of reality by simplifying and abstracting them into manageable form. It is made by human cognition as an instrument of knowledge production and communication.

Abbreviation is the human-made practice of producing a shortened form of a word, phrase, or name for efficient repeated use in writing or speech — a conventionally agreed signal that stands in for a longer form.

A procedure is the human-made construction of a structured sequence of steps designed to achieve a specific outcome consistently — a recipe for action that persists across instances through documentation, training, or institutional memory. Built to standardize and make repeatable what would otherwise be ad hoc.

A loanword is a word or term borrowed from one language and incorporated into another, with conventions governing its phonological, morphological, and semantic adaptation. The borrowing process is a human-made linguistic practice, sustained by bilingual communities, translation work, and the natural contact between cultures.

Normalization is the human-made practice of establishing and applying standards to bring diverse items into conformity. It carves a process: identify a norm or standard, measure deviation, and adjust toward alignment. The persistence mechanism is institutional enforcement — through law, convention, or automated systems — that sustains the standard across time and scale.

A process is a human-made sequence of ordered actions designed to transform inputs into outputs through a repeatable, traceable flow. It carves a structured transformation: a bounded set of steps, each with defined inputs/outputs, arranged in a controlled sequence that can be executed, monitored, and reproduced by humans or human-designed systems.

Gatekeeping is the human-made practice of controlling or regulating access to a resource, group, territory, or body of knowledge. It is an institutional mechanism — rules, norms, credentials, or thresholds — that determines who may enter, participate, or benefit. Gatekeeping exists wherever a community or system draws a boundary between insiders and outsiders, and enforces it through criteria, rituals, or power.

Abundance is the human-made economic and social construct describing states where resources, goods, or opportunities exceed demand — the conceptual opposite of scarcity, used as a planning frame, policy goal, and cultural ideal.

A workflow is a human-made sequence of interlinked processes, tasks, or steps organized to produce a defined output. It specifies the order of operations, the actors or systems involved at each stage, and the handoffs between them — a structured choreography of work that persists through documentation, software, or institutional memory.

Aesthetic is the human-made framework for evaluating beauty, taste, and artistic merit. It is a constructed set of criteria and principles — shaped by culture, history, and discipline — that enables humans to judge, classify, and communicate about sensory and intellectual experience. The self is an entry; the beauty itself is not.

A maxim is a human-made concise statement of a general truth or guiding principle, crafted for memorability and transmitted through teaching, repetition, and cultural preservation. It is a linguistic artifact — the map of condensed wisdom, not the wisdom itself.

Information architecture is the human-made practice of organizing, structuring, and labeling information within digital and physical environments to support usability, findability, and comprehension. It is built through taxonomy design, navigation systems, and metadata schemas, persisted via documentation, design systems, and implementation in software and physical spaces.

Controlled-vocabulary is a human-made system for representing information using a predefined set of terms, designed to ensure consistency in indexing, searching, and retrieving documents or data across a collection. It persists through formal standardization bodies and is maintained as a living document within information systems.

A data-model is a human-made abstraction that organizes data elements, defines their relationships, and constrains how data can be created, stored, updated, and accessed within a system. It serves as a blueprint for data architecture in information systems, database design, and software engineering.

Homeostasis is a human-made concept — the conceptual framework developed by Walter Cannon in 1926 to describe how systems maintain stability through self-regulating feedback loops. The concept maps natural regulatory phenomena (from physiological thermoregulation to organizational adaptation) into a formalizable structure. It persists through scientific practice: taught in biology, psychology, and systems theory; applied in engineering, ecology, and cybernetics; refined through decades of research from Cannon's original work to Ashby's laws of requisite variety. The entry names the MAP of self-regulation, not the natural processes themselves.

A human-made form of expression — a concise, stylistically crafted statement that observes a truth about the human condition or natural world. Unlike maxims (which prescribe conduct), aphorisms describe or illuminate. They are authored literary artifacts, transmitted through writing, quotation, and citation, persisting as a recognized rhetorical form in literature, philosophy, and everyday speech.

A human-made practice of deliberately concealing meaning — through language, design, or representation — to make information harder to understand, interpret, or discover. It persists through documents, code, speech, and artifacts that encode ambiguity as a feature, maintained by the actors who produce and sustain it.

A living taxonomy of human-made concepts — a network of entries and edges that maps everything humans make: objects, institutions, practices, words, and ideas. Built to persist as a growing, self-correcting web of knowledge where each construct is defined by its parameters, persistence mechanism, and relations to other constructs.

A human-made concept for a belief or understanding that contradicts established reality or evidence. It is the map of error — the category humans built to identify, discuss, and correct faulty understanding — built to persist through teaching and communication as a tool for intellectual hygiene.

The human-made concept of apparent positional shift when an object is observed from different vantage points, formalized as a measurement technique and extended metaphorically across disciplines to denote how understanding changes with perspective. It is the map of perspective-dependent observation — the framework humans built to quantify, reason about, and apply viewpoint-dependent displacement.

A human-made framework for categorizing, structuring, and making information accessible. Built to persist through taxonomies, indexes, ontologies, and classification schemas — the deliberate ordering of knowledge so that it can be found, navigated, and extended by others.

The human-made concept distinguishing actual outcomes from expected or prescribed ones. Built to track, classify, and learn from deviation — the foundational construct for quality control, debugging, verification, and all forms of corrective reasoning across every domain of human practice.

A human-made form of terse expression conveying a traditional piece of wisdom or general truth. Built to persist through oral tradition, written compilation, and cultural transmission — the distilled verdict of collective experience, distinguished from novel aphorism by its age and communal endorsement.

A human-made form of brief, witty expression, typically in verse, that states a pointed observation or idea. Built to persist through literary tradition, anthologies, and quotational use — a linguistic artifact refined for impact over duration.

Human-made social customs that regulate behavior through shared practice and collective enforcement. Built to persist through cultural transmission, socialization, and the reputation costs of violation — a framework of expected conduct that holds communities together.

A human-made temporary support structure — literal (construction) or figurative (education, programming, organizational design) — built to enable the development of something that could not yet stand on its own. Persisted through practice, technical documentation, and pedagogical transmission.

Human-made conceptual framework for understanding how scientific and cultural worldviews change — coined by Thomas Kuhn to describe the replacement of one dominant conceptual scheme with another. Built to persist through academic discourse, history of science, and cultural analysis.

Human-made systematic process for identifying problems, conditions, or causes through evidence-based analysis — from medical diagnosis to technical fault-finding. Persists through diagnostic manuals (ICD, SNOMED), medical education, and standardized classification systems.

Human-made concept for an irrational belief in causal connections between unrelated actions or events, often involving supernatural agency. Persists through cultural transmission, ritual practice, and oral tradition — distinguishing it from rational causal reasoning.

Human-made psychological concept describing the need for a stable, coherent sense of self and world-order. Persists through therapeutic practice, philosophical discourse, and social rituals that maintain existential confidence.

Human-made rhetorical practice of vividly describing visual artworks in words — transforming static images into temporal narrative through language. Persists through art criticism, literary tradition, museum cataloging, and pedagogy.

Human-made practice of constructing an artificial model to imitate the behavior of a real or proposed system, enabling prediction, testing, and understanding without operating on the actual system. Persists through scientific computing, engineering design, military training, and educational pedagogy.

Human-made concept identifying a property or quantity that remains unchanged when specific transformations or operations are applied to a system. Persists through mathematics, physics, computer science, and formal reasoning as a tool for isolating essential structure amid change.

Human-made representation in which relationships between elements in a source domain are mapped onto relationships in a target domain through structural or functional similarity. Persists through scientific modeling, engineering design, educational tools, and cognitive practice as a means of reasoning about the unfamiliar by way of the familiar.

Human-made discipline that studies how agents allocate scarce resources among competing ends. Persists through academic institutions, textbooks, and formal training that transmit its methods and theories across generations.

Human-made limitation that restricts the space of possible actions, configurations, or outcomes within a system. Persists through formal rules, engineering specifications, design constraints, legal provisions, and social agreements that channel behavior and structure possibility.

Signaling is the human practice of producing observable cues to convey information, influence behavior, or establish status. It is built by cultural convention, economic incentive, and social learning — not a natural phenomenon. Signaling persists through repeated patterns of interpretation and response across communities, institutions, and markets.

The existing state of affairs in a social, political, or organizational context, treated as a baseline or reference point against which change is measured. It is a human-made construct: there is no natural status quo — the concept arises only when humans designate a current arrangement as the default position and orient debate, policy, or behavior around preserving or altering it.

A human-made representational artifact that formalizes how people think, reason, and make decisions within a domain. Built by researchers, designers, and AI engineers to model, predict, and improve human cognition in specific contexts. Persists through documentation, software implementations, and pedagogical teaching.

A human-made social construct: a customary pattern of behavior that a community treats as proper or normal, enforced through informal social sanction rather than formal rules or moral weight. Distinguished from mores by its lack of moral significance — folkways govern etiquette, dress, greeting, and routine conduct; violating them draws disapproval but not outrage.
A human-made pattern of repeated behavior — a structured sequence of actions performed regularly, designed to reduce decision cost and stabilize social or personal practice
A human-made cognitive construct: a settled disposition to approach situations in a particular way, shaped by experience and belief, that filters perception and guides interpretation

A human-made concept specifying the limiting conditions under which a system, model, or process operates correctly. It defines the range of parameters — such as initial values, environmental limits, or resource caps — that must hold for the system to function as intended, and beyond which it fails or behaves unpredictably.

A human-made construct in which one thing is treated as standing for something else to someone — the fundamental unit of semiotic meaning, maintained through social agreement and cultural transmission.

A naming-convention is a human-made agreement on how to name items within a domain — it standardizes labels to reduce ambiguity and enable reliable reference. It is built by human practice and persists through repeated use, documentation, and enforcement within a community or system.

A standard-operating-procedure is a human-made written document that specifies the exact steps for carrying out a routine operation, ensuring consistency, safety, and quality. It is built by organizational design and persists through documentation systems and training practices.

A mind-map is a human-made visual diagram that organizes information hierarchically using nodes and connecting branches, built for thinking, planning, and communication. It persists through documentation and teaching.
